title: Medicare Part B Premium 2026 and IRMAA Brackets
metaDescription: The standard Medicare Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90, with a $283 deductible. See how 2026 IRMAA brackets and surcharges affect your monthly cost.
h1: Medicare Part B Premium 2026 and IRMAA Brackets
cardBlurb: Learn the standard 2026 Medicare Part B premium, the annual deductible, and how IRMAA income tiers increase monthly costs.
introText:
The standard Medicare Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90 each month, and the annual Part B deductible is $283. At ModernWallet, we treat the cost of this coverage as a line item to price before anything else in a retirement budget.

Higher-income enrollees pay an additional surcharge known as the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA). Roughly 8% of people enrolled in Part B pay this extra charge, which raises both Part B and Part D monthly costs. Social Security calculates whether you owe an adjustment using a past federal tax return, generally evaluating the return filed in 2025 for the 2024 tax year.

sections.heading: Medicare Part B Premium 2026 and Deductible Amounts
sections.body:
The standard monthly Medicare Part B premium for 2026 is $202.90, which covers outpatient medical services, doctor visits, and preventive care. Over a full calendar year of 12 months, that base monthly charge totals $2,434.80 per beneficiary.

Enrollees also pay an annual Part B deductible of $283 in 2026 before Medicare coverage begins paying for outpatient services. Combining 12 monthly payments of $202.90 with the $283 deductible results in a base annual Part B cash outlay of $2,717.80.

Hospital inpatient care falls under Medicare Part A. The Part A inpatient hospital deductible for 2026 is $1,736 per benefit period admission. While most retirees qualify for premium-free Part A through their payroll work history, that $1,736 deductible applies whenever an individual is admitted to a hospital inpatient room.

sections.heading: Income Adjustments Under the IRMAA Rules
sections.body:
An Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA) is a statutory monthly surcharge added to standard Part B and Part D premiums for higher-income beneficiaries. The adjustment is established by the [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/2026-medicare-parts-b-premiums-deductibles) to scale Medicare financing based on reported household income.

Federal data shows that IRMAA affects roughly 8% of people with Medicare Part B. The remaining 92% of beneficiaries pay only the standard $202.90 monthly rate.

Social Security determines your bracket using the most recent federal income tax return available. For 2026 coverage, Social Security generally assesses the tax return filed in 2025 for the 2024 tax year. If your household income has changed, confirm your active filing records and review options directly with Social Security.

sections.heading: Surcharges Beyond the Standard Medicare Part B Premium 2026
sections.body:
Medicare divides Part B and Part D premiums across six income brackets based on modified adjusted gross income. Each tier specifies a monthly Part B surcharge and a monthly Part D surcharge that get added to standard plan costs.

Tier 1 applies to individual filers earning $109,000 or less and married couples filing jointly earning $218,000 or less. These enrollees pay a $0.00 adjustment, leaving their monthly Part B premium at the standard $202.90 and their Part D adjustment at $0.00.

Tier 2 applies to individual income above $109,000 to $137,000 and joint income above $218,000 to $274,000. Beneficiaries in this bracket pay an $81.20 Part B adjustment, bringing their total Part B premium to $284.10 per month, plus a $14.50 monthly Part D adjustment.

Tier 3 covers individual income above $137,000 to $171,000 and joint income above $274,000 to $342,000. This tier adds a $202.90 Part B adjustment for a total monthly Part B payment of $405.80, alongside a $37.50 monthly Part D adjustment.

Tier 4 covers individual income above $171,000 to $205,000 and joint income above $342,000 to $410,000. Enrollees in this tier face a $324.60 Part B adjustment, creating a total monthly Part B premium of $527.50, plus a $60.40 monthly Part D adjustment.

Tier 5 applies to individual income above $205,000 to under $500,000 and joint income above $410,000 to under $750,000. The monthly Part B adjustment is $446.30, raising the total Part B premium to $649.20 per month, with an $83.30 monthly Part D adjustment.

Tier 6 applies to individual income of $500,000 or more and joint income of $750,000 or more. Beneficiaries pay a $487.00 Part B adjustment for a total monthly Part B premium of $689.90, alongside a $91.00 monthly Part D adjustment.

The joint income limits apply specifically to couples who are married filing jointly. Joint thresholds do not double the single limits at every level, as the top joint bracket begins at $750,000 rather than $1,000,000. Other tax filing statuses follow distinct rules that you should confirm directly with Social Security.

sections.heading: Threshold Cliffs and Common Income Triggers
sections.body:
Income brackets for IRMAA function as strict cliffs where a single dollar of income pushes an enrollee into the next higher tier. Because the brackets apply to income above each threshold, an individual reporting $109,001 in income triggers the full Tier 2 surcharge.

Crossing into Tier 2 adds $81.20 per month to your Part B bill ($974.40 per year) and $14.50 per month to your Part D bill ($174.00 per year). That single dollar of additional income results in $1,148.40 in extra annual Medicare expenses across both parts.

Common retirement financial moves can unexpectedly elevate modified adjusted gross income. Large traditional retirement account distributions, realized capital gains from taxable investment accounts, or taxable Roth conversions like those explained in our guide to [Roth conversion rules](/guides/roth-conversion-rules/) all count toward your income totals.

Before scheduling large asset sales or retirement account withdrawals, check the numbers against the published brackets. You can project ongoing portfolio cash flows using our [retirement income calculator](/retirement/retirement-income-calculator/) to anticipate potential bracket shifts.

sections.heading: Expenses Outside Basic Part B Coverage
sections.body:
The standard Part B premium and deductible do not represent the total cost of healthcare for most retirees. Medicare enrollees typically purchase supplemental insurance or private plan alternatives to manage cost-sharing responsibilities.

Retirees choosing between private coverage structures often compare [Medicare vs Medicare Advantage](/compare/medicare-vs-medicare-advantage/) to evaluate network restrictions and monthly outlays. Those who stay in original Medicare often compare [Medicare Advantage vs Medigap](/compare/medicare-advantage-vs-medigap/) to determine whether a supplemental policy fits their budget.

Private plan premiums, prescription drug plan premiums, and copayments vary widely by insurer and zip code. You can compare plan options and verify drug formularies on Medicare.gov. When IRMAA applies, your Part D adjustment is billed on top of whatever base premium your private prescription drug plan charges.

sections.heading: Next Steps for the Medicare Part B Premium 2026
sections.body:
Review the annual notice sent by Social Security each autumn to confirm your exact Part B premium and IRMAA status for the upcoming year. That notice confirms whether your reported tax return placed you into an income surcharge tier for 2026.

If your notice reflects an adjustment, verify that the underlying income numbers match the tax return on file for that assessment year. Enrollees planning their overall transition timeline can review our guide on [Medicare enrollment periods](/guides/medicare-enrollment-periods/) or model claim dates with our [Social Security retirement calculator](/retirement/social-security-retirement-calculator/).

The information on this page serves general educational purposes and does not provide individualized tax, financial, or healthcare advice. Premium schedules and regulatory thresholds are established by federal authorities. Consult a licensed insurance professional, certified public accountant, or financial advisor to determine the next steps for your Medicare Part B premium 2026 and personal retirement plan.

faqs.question: What is the Medicare Part B premium in 2026?
faqs.answer: The standard monthly Medicare Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90. Most beneficiaries pay this base rate, while roughly 8% pay a higher premium due to an income-related monthly adjustment.

faqs.question: What is the Part B deductible in 2026?
faqs.answer: The annual Part B deductible in 2026 is $283. Beneficiaries must pay this amount out of pocket for covered outpatient services before Medicare Part B begins paying its share.

faqs.question: What income triggers IRMAA in 2026?
faqs.answer: An income above $109,000 for individual tax filers or above $218,000 for married couples filing jointly triggers IRMAA in 2026. Beneficiaries with modified adjusted gross income at or below those amounts pay only the standard premium.

faqs.question: Do married couples have higher IRMAA thresholds?
faqs.answer: Yes, married couples filing jointly have higher income thresholds than single filers, starting above $218,000 in 2026. However, the joint thresholds do not double the single limits across all tiers, capping at $750,000 or more for the highest tier compared to $500,000 for individuals.

faqs.question: Is the Part D IRMAA separate from the Part B IRMAA?
faqs.answer: Yes, Part D IRMAA is an additional monthly surcharge applied to your prescription drug plan premium. It uses the same income tiers as Part B, adding between $14.50 and $91.00 per month to your drug plan cost depending on your income tier.
